Lecture start

Review: Classification + Rubella Virus

Baltimore classification p. 1

  • David Baltimore founded a non-phylogenetic classification based on genome type and method of replication.
  • Groups
    • Group 1: double-stranded DNA viruses
    • Group 2: single-stranded DNA viruses
    • Group 3: double-stranded RNA viruses
    • Group 4: positive-sense single-stranded RNA viruses
    • Group 5: negative-sense single-stranded RNA viruses
    • Group 6: single-stranded reverse-transcribing RNA viruses
    • Group 7: double-stranded reverse-transcribing DNA viruses

RNA virus pattern p. 2

  • Almost all RNA viruses are single-stranded.
  • Reoviridae is the lecture exception because it is double-stranded.
  • Segmented genomes have a higher tendency to undergo mutations.
  • Group III and non-enveloped Group IV viruses are transmitted by the fecal-oral or foodborne route according to the lecture.

Togaviridae and Matonaviridae classification p. 2

FamilyGenusLecture examples / note
TogaviridaeAlphavirusArthropod-borne. Mosquito vectors. Chikungunya, Eastern Equine Encephalitis, Western Equine Encephalitis, Venezuelan Equine Encephalitis, Mayaro, O’Nyong-nyong, Ross River.
MatonaviridaeRubivirusRubella virus. Morphologically similar to togaviruses but not arthropod-transmitted.

Rubella virus: structure and antigenic features p. 2

  • Single-stranded, positive-sense, nonsegmented, enveloped virus.
  • Sole member of genus Rubivirus in Matonaviridae.
  • One serotype identified.
  • Classified into 2 related clades and 9 genotypes.
  • Three immunogenic antigens
    • E1 envelope antigen
    • E2 envelope antigen
    • C capsid antigen
  • The lecture figure also labels the ssRNA genome.

Postnatal rubella: pathogenesis and timing p. 2

Respiratory droplet / direct contact→Upper respiratory mucosa→Initial respiratory replication→Cervical lymph node multiplication→Viremia at 7–9 days→Antibody appears at day 13–15 with rash
  • Incubation period: 12 days or longer.
  • After the rash appears, virus remains detectable mainly in the nasopharynx and may persist for several weeks.
  • 20–50% of primary infections are subclinical.
  • Appearance of antibody coincides with rash, supporting an immunologic basis for the rash in the lecture.

Postnatal rubella: clinical findings and immunity p. 3

  • Malaise, low-grade fever, and morbilliform rash can appear on the same day.
  • Rash starts on the face, extends over trunk and extremities, and rarely lasts more than 3 days.
  • No rash feature is pathognomonic for rubella.
  • Rubella antibodies appear as the rash fades. Titers rise 1–3 weeks later.
  • IgM is the initial antibody and does not persist beyond 6 weeks.
  • IgG persists for life.
  • One attack gives lifelong immunity because there is one antigenic type.
  • Maternal antibodies protect offspring for about 4–6 months.

Rubella laboratory diagnosis p. 3

TestSpecimenWhen to collect / interpretation
RT-PCRNP or throat swabIdeally 0–3 days after rash onset. May be collected up to 7 days.
RT-PCRUrineWithin 7 days of rash onset. Collecting urine with NP/OP swab may improve sensitivity near the end of the detection window.
IgMSerumMost sensitive at 4+ days after rash onset. May be detected for 30 days after acute rubella.
IgGSerumUsed for evidence of immunity. Can be detected around 2 weeks after MMR vaccination.
Must Know: Rubella Serology p. 3
IgG is the only test for immunity.
Rubella-specific IgM appears after primary infection or vaccination.
Rubella-specific IgG is detectable from day 4 after rash onset and peaks around 1–2 weeks.

Congenital rubella syndrome: pathogenesis p. 3

Maternal viremia during pregnancy→Placental and fetal infection→Limited fetal cells infected→Reduced growth rate of infected cells→Deranged and hypoplastic organ development→Structural anomalies
Timing Determines Damage p. 3
Earlier pregnancy → greater fetal damage because organogenesis is occurring.
After the 20th week, birth defects are uncommon in the lecture.
Defect groupExamples from the lecture

Ocular defects such as congenital cataracts

Congenital rubella diagnosis and prevention p. 4

  • Maternal IgG crosses to the infant and is lost over about 6 months.
  • Infant IgM supports congenital infection because IgM does not cross the placenta and must have been synthesized by the infant in utero.
  • The lecture notes impaired cell-mediated immunity specific for rubella.
  • Live attenuated rubella vaccine: a single dose gives more than 95% long-lasting immunity.
  • Available as monovalent rubella or in combinations such as MR, MMR, and MMRV.
Coronaviridae

Coronaviruses and SARS-CoV-2

Classification p. 4

  • Single-stranded, positive-sense, nonsegmented, enveloped.
  • Order: Nidovirales.
  • Family: Coronaviridae.
  • Subfamilies: Torovirinae and Coronavirinae.
  • Coronavirinae genera
    • Alphacoronavirus: HCoV-229E, HCoV-NL63
    • Betacoronavirus: SARS-CoV-1, SARS-CoV-2, MERS-CoV, HCoV-OC43, HCoV-HKU1
    • Gammacoronavirus
    • Deltacoronavirus
  • Human coronaviruses belong to the Alpha and Beta coronaviruses.
  • The lecture lists common colds, lower respiratory tract infections, and gastroenteritis in infants as diseases caused by human coronaviruses.

Hosts and host receptors p. 5

SARS-CoVBatsCivet catsACE-2

Lecture-Specific Note p. 5
The appendix contains broader SARS, MERS, and COVID-19 data. The lecture text states that the lecturer focused only on hosts and receptors for those comparisons.

SARS-CoV-2 transmission p. 5

  • Crowded spaces facilitate easier human-to-human transmission.

SARS-CoV-2 replication p. 5

S protein binds ACE2→Internalization by absorptive endocytosis or membrane fusion→Viral RNA released into cytoplasm→Translation into polyproteins→Polyprotein cleavage→Replication-transcription complex→Genomic replication + subgenomic transcription→S, E, M translation→Assembly in ERGIC→Envelope acquisition and release
  • The replication cycle occurs in the cytoplasm.
  • S glycoprotein is described as the most potent determinant for viral entry.
  • Target cells listed include the lungs, heart, and kidneys.
  • Antiviral agents target key stages of the replication cycle according to the lecture.
Must Know: Coronavirus Assembly p. 5
Structural proteins S, E, and M are translated and assemble with the nucleocapsid in the ER-Golgi intermediate compartment (ERGIC).
New virions acquire their envelope there before release.

Host immune response to SARS-CoV-2 p. 5

Infection→Innate + adaptive activation→Predominantly Th1-mediated response→CD8+ CTLs, CD4+ helper T cells, B-cell antibodies
  • B cells produce neutralizing antibodies that protect against infection and prevent reinfection in the lecture.
  • Excessive innate and adaptive activation raises cytokines and chemokines and is associated with disease severity.
  • Cytokine storm can lead to lymphopenia through T-cell necrosis or apoptosis.
  • The inflammatory response initiates viral sepsis, then inflammation-induced lung injury and other complications.
  • More severe disease is associated with lower circulating B cells, CD4+ cells, and CD8+ cells.

Paramyxoviridae

Classification, Structure, Replication, and Shared Cytopathic Effects

Classification p. 6

SubfamilyGenusHuman viruses
ParamyxovirinaeRespirovirusParainfluenza virus 1 and 3
ParamyxovirinaeRubulavirusMumps virus
Parainfluenza virus 2, 4a, 4b
ParamyxovirinaeMorbillivirusMeasles virus
ParamyxovirinaeHenipavirusHendra virus
Nipah virus
PneumovirinaePneumovirusRespiratory syncytial virus
PneumovirinaeMetapneumovirusHuman metapneumovirus
  • Group 5 Baltimore classification.
  • -ssRNA, nonsegmented, enveloped.
  • Most members are monotypic and all are described as antigenically stable.
  • The lecture notes relation to Rhabdoviridae, Bornaviridae, and Filoviridae.

Structure and key proteins p. 6

  • Matrix protein, fusion protein, and hemagglutinin-neuraminidase are highlighted.
  • HN, H, and G proteins function as attachment proteins.
  • Fusion protein produces giant cells or syncytial cells.
  • Attachment glycoprotein plus fusion protein allow cell attachment, host entry, and fusion of adjacent cells.
Must Know: Fusion Protein p. 6
The fusion protein forms giant cells or syncytial cells, which are important recognition features of paramyxovirus infection.

Attachment, penetration, and uncoating p. 6

HN, H, or G binds host cell→F0 cleaved to active F1→F1 refolds at neutral pH→Viral envelope fuses with cell membrane→Nucleocapsid released directly into cell
  • Measles receptor: CD46 or CD150 molecule.
  • F0 cleavage is essential. Without cleavage, fusion and infection cannot occur.
  • This entry pathway allows paramyxoviruses to bypass internalization through endosomes.

Transcription, translation, and RNA replication p. 6

  • Because the genome is negative-sense RNA, the viral RNA polymerase transcribes mRNAs in the cytoplasm without requiring nuclear functions or primers.
  • Viral proteins are made in the cytoplasm. Glycoproteins are glycosylated through the secretory pathway.
  • The genome is nonsegmented, preventing the gene segment reshuffling seen in influenza.
  • HN/H/G and F proteins show minimal antigenic variation over time.
  • RNA polymerase is error-prone, but the lecture states that many mutations are not tolerated because of structural and functional constraints.
Key Differentiator p. 6
Paramyxoviruses do not undergo antigenic drift.
This is presented as a primary difference from Orthomyxoviruses.

Maturation p. 6

  • Virions mature by budding from the cell surface.
  • Progeny nucleocapsids form in the cytoplasm and move to membrane regions containing viral HN/H/G and F0 spikes.
  • M protein links the viral envelope to the nucleocapsid and is essential for particle formation.
  • Most host proteins are excluded during budding.
  • Neuraminidase activity is present in the HN protein of parainfluenza and mumps viruses and prevents self-aggregation.
  • Neuraminidase activity is absent in other paramyxoviruses according to the lecture.

Syncytium formation and inclusion bodies p. 7

  • Infected cells display F0 on the cell surface.
  • Host proteases activate F0. Activated fusion protein fuses adjacent cell membranes.
  • This creates large multinucleated syncytia and supports cell-to-cell spread.
  • Acidophilic cytoplasmic inclusions are regularly formed.
  • Inclusion bodies are sites of viral synthesis and contain recognizable nucleocapsid and viral proteins.
  • The lecture notes that RNA viruses replicate in the cytoplasm.
  • Measles also produces intranuclear inclusions.
Must Know: Paramyxovirus Cytopathic Pattern p. 7
Syncytium formation is a hallmark and common response to paramyxovirus infection.
Inclusion bodies are sites of viral synthesis.
Respirovirus / Rubulavirus

Human Parainfluenza Virus

Pathogenesis and disease by type p. 7

TypeDepth / site of diseaseKey clinical pattern
GeneralRespiratory epithelium. Viremia uncommon or absent.May remain in nose and throat and cause common cold syndrome.
Type 1 and 2Larynx and upper tracheaCroup or laryngotracheobronchitis. Common in young children, especially 6–18 months. Characteristic barking cough.
Type 3Lower trachea and bronchiPneumonia or bronchiolitis, especially in young infants under 6 months.
Type 4Usually milderUsually not serious even on first infection. Most common complication is otitis media.
Croup Pattern p. 7
Respiratory obstruction results from swelling of the larynx and related structures.
The lecture labels the cough as a characteristic barking cough.

Newcastle disease virus p. 7

  • Avian paramyxovirus.
  • Can cause conjunctival inflammation in humans.
  • Presented as an occupational disease in workers handling infected birds.

Immunity p. 7

  • Parainfluenza types 1, 2, and 3 are distinct serotypes without significant cross-neutralization.
  • Maternal antibodies and antibodies from prior infection do not prevent infection or reinfection.
  • These antibodies can modify disease severity, often producing a nonfebrile URTI.
  • Secretory IgA gives short-term protection.
  • Reinfections are common even in adults.
  • Serum antibodies are produced against both HN and F surface proteins.
  • Repeated infections can make serology harder to interpret because of shared antigenic determinants with viruses such as mumps.

Laboratory diagnosis p. 7

MethodLecture use
NAAT / RT-PCRPreferred diagnostic method. Detects viral RNA in NP swabs, washes, or aspirates.
Viral isolationPresented as the definitive diagnosis from appropriate specimens.
Antigen detectionRapid diagnosis using exfoliated nasopharyngeal cells and direct or indirect immunofluorescence.
SerologyPaired acute and convalescent sera. A four-fold rise in antibody level supports infection. Neutralization, HI, or ELISA may be used.
Must Know: Epidemiology p. 7
Parainfluenza type 3 is the most prevalent.
About two-thirds of infants are infected during the first year of life. By age 2, children already have antibodies.
Types 1 and 2 are less prevalent. Infection is generally acquired before age 5.
Transmission is by direct person-to-person contact or large droplet aerosols.
The lecture highlights spread among school children and hospitals.
Rubulavirus

Mumps Virus

Pathogenesis and target organs p. 8

Upper respiratory epithelial replication→Regional lymph node infection→Viremia→Salivary glands + other organs
  • Humans are the only natural hosts.
  • Systemic inflammation can involve salivary glands, testes, ovaries, pancreas, mammary glands, and CNS.
  • Parotid involvement is not obligatory. Mumps can occur without parotitis.
  • Submandibular glands may also be involved.

Transmission timing and parotitis p. 8

  • Incubation period: 14–18 days.
  • Virus is shed in saliva from 3 days before to 9 days after onset of parotid or salivary gland swelling.
  • About one-third have inapparent infections and can still shed virus.
  • Control is difficult because of the long and variable incubation, presymptomatic saliva shedding, and many asymptomatic infectious cases.
  • Parotid swelling is described as painful inflammation between the earlobe and angle of the mandible.

Clinical findings and postpubertal complications p. 8

  • One-third are subclinical. This is especially common in children under 2 years.
  • Parotid or other salivary gland swelling and pain.
  • CNS involvement: 10–30%. Aseptic meningitis may occur and may spontaneously resolve.
  • After puberty, the testes or ovaries may be affected.
  • Males may develop unilateral orchitis. Pain is attributed to swelling of the inflamed testis within the tight tunica albuginea.

Symptoms p. 8

  • Pain in front of the neck or in front of the ears.
  • Trouble chewing.
  • Testicular pain and tenderness in males.
  • Fever, headache, muscle aches, tiredness, and loss of appetite.

Immunity p. 8

  • Permanent immunity after a single infection.
  • Only one antigenic type. No antigenic variation.
  • HN glycoprotein antibodies develop slowly, around 4 weeks after onset, and persist for years.
  • NP nucleocapsid antibodies appear earliest, around 3–7 days after symptom onset, and disappear within 6 months.
  • Subclinical infection can still generate lifelong immunity.
  • Passive maternal immunity makes mumps rare in infants younger than 6 months.

Laboratory diagnosis and prevention p. 8

AreaLecture points
RT-PCRDetects mumps genome sequences in clinical samples.
SerologyELISA or HI. A single mumps antibody result is not adequate to diagnose infection. Use paired sera and look for a four-fold rise.
IgMPresent in early illness until about 60 days. Supports recent infection.
IgGMeans prior mumps exposure in the lecture.
PreventionLive attenuated mumps vaccine. Produces a subclinical noncommunicable infection. Commonly given as MMR.
Morbillivirus

Measles Virus (Rubeola)

Do Not Confuse p. 8
Measles virus = Rubeola.
Rubella = German measles.

Pathogenesis p. 9

Respiratory tract replication→Regional lymph nodes→Primary viremia→Reticuloendothelial replication→Secondary viremia→Skin, respiratory tract, conjunctiva
  • Humans are the only natural host.
  • Secondary viremia seeds epithelial surfaces, producing focal replication including skin rash.
  • Patients are contagious during the prodrome and the first 2–5 days of rash. Virus can be present in tears, nasal and throat secretions, urine, and blood.
  • The maculopapular rash appears around day 14, when circulating antibodies become detectable.
Must Know: Rash and Antibody p. 9
The measles rash appears when circulating antibodies become detectable.
The lecture uses an incubation period of about 2 weeks.

Natural history p. 9

Prodrome and Koplik spots p. 9

  • Prodrome: fever, sneezing, coughing, runny nose, photophobia or eye redness, and lymphonemia as written in the lecture.
  • Koplik spots are pathognomonic for measles.
  • They are small bluish-white ulcerations on the buccal mucosa opposite the lower molars.
  • They appear slightly before the rash.
  • Scrapings contain giant cells.

Measles rash p. 9

  • Begins on the head and moves progressively downward to chest, trunk, and limbs.
  • Starts as discrete pink maculopapules.
  • Lesions coalesce into blotches and become brownish within 5–10 days.

Complications p. 9

ComplicationLecture detail
Otitis mediaMost common complication.
PneumoniaMost common life-threatening complication. Commonly from secondary bacterial infection.
Giant cell pneumoniaSerious complication in alveoli among children and adults with cell-mediated immune deficiencies. Giant cells indicate adjacent infected cells and impaired alveolar function.
Acute encephalitisOccurs in about 1:1000 cases.
Acute disseminated encephalomyelitisAutoimmune disease associated with immune response to myelin.
APMEAcute post-infectious measles encephalitis.
MIBEMeasles inclusion body encephalitis.
SSPERare complication developing years after initial measles. Large amounts of measles antigen are present in inclusion bodies of infected brain cells. The lecture groups measles with slow viruses because of SSPE.
Must Know: Measles Complications p. 9
Most common complication: otitis media.
Most common life-threatening complication: pneumonia from secondary bacterial infection.
SSPE is the rare delayed complication developing years after infection.

Immunity and immune suppression p. 10

  • Only one antigenic type.
  • Infection confers lifelong immunity.
  • Protective immunity is attributed to neutralizing antibodies against the H protein.
  • Measles causes immune suppression, which can promote serious secondary bacterial infection.
  • Immune suppression may persist for months as the leukocyte count decreases.

Laboratory diagnosis p. 10

MethodLecture detail
RT-PCR / antigen detectionEpithelial cells from respiratory secretions, nasopharynx, conjunctiva, and urine.
SerologyELISA and HI. Look for a four-fold rise in antibody titer.
Virus isolationMonkey or human kidney cells. Look for multinucleated giant cells with intranuclear and intracytoplasmic inclusion bodies.

Prevention and control p. 10

  • Live attenuated measles vaccine is used in combination with rubella and mumps as MMR.
  • The lecture states that MMR may be given as early as 9 months old.
Henipavirus

Nipah and Hendra Viruses

Nipah virus: origin and epidemiology p. 10

  • The name Nipah came from a Malaysian village.
  • Nipah disease can spread between animals and people.
  • Pteropus fruit bats, or flying foxes, carry the virus.
  • First recognized in 1999 during an outbreak in pigs and people in Malaysia and Singapore.
  • The lecture notes around 300 illnesses and more than 100 deaths in that outbreak.
  • In the first outbreak, bats spread virus to pigs, then people working closely with infected pigs became ill.
  • Reported outbreak countries listed are Bangladesh, India, Malaysia, Philippines, and Singapore.
  • Fruit bats carrying Nipah occur throughout Asia, the South Pacific, and Australia, so cases may occur even where outbreaks have not been reported.

Nipah: signs, symptoms, and spread p. 11

  • Symptom onset: about 4–14 days after infection.
  • Typical illness may last 3–14 days with fever, headache, cough, sore throat, and difficulty breathing.
  • Encephalitis may occur later and cause confusion, drowsiness, seizures, and coma within 24–48 hours in severe cases.
  • Transmission routes
    • Direct contact with infected animals such as bats or pigs
    • Food or drinks contaminated by infected animals, including fruit or raw date palm sap
    • Close contact with body fluids of an infected person
  • Spillover event: initial spread from animal to a person.
  • After human infection, the virus can spread person to person.

Nipah: reducing risk p. 11

Transmission interfaceLecture risk-reduction measures
Bat → humanWash hands regularly
Avoid flying fox bats and sick pigs
Avoid bat roosts
Avoid items soiled by bats
Avoid raw date palm sap or fruit that could be soiled by bats
Animal → humanWear gloves and protective clothing when handling sick animals or tissues and during slaughter or culling
Avoid contact with infected pigs
In endemic areas, consider fruit bats when planning new pig farms and protect pig feed and sheds from bats
Human → humanAvoid close unprotected physical contact with infected people
Wash hands after caring for or visiting sick people

Hendra virus: epidemiology and transmission p. 12

  • First identified in a 1994 outbreak of lung and brain disease in horses and people in Hendra, Australia.
  • Pteropus flying foxes maintain Hendra virus in nature.
  • The virus has been found in all four species of Australian flying foxes.
  • Flying foxes can infect horses through bites or exposure to infected bat urine, droppings, or saliva.
  • Spread from flying foxes to horses is described as limited to coastal and forested regions of Queensland and New South Wales.
  • Horses can then spread virus to people.
  • The lecture states that only seven human cases had been reported.
  • The lecture also lists species-to-species transmission as horse-to-horse and human-to-human.

Hendra: symptoms and pathogenesis p. 12

  • Symptoms begin 9–16 days after contact with an infected horse.
  • Can cause lung problems with severe flu-like symptoms.
  • Some cases progress to encephalitis.
  • The lecture gives a fatality figure of 57%.
  • Henipavirus pathogenesis in the figure
    • Initial stage affects respiratory tract, especially bronchi and alveoli, with inflammatory mediator release
    • Second stage disseminates virus through the bloodstream, free or leukocyte-associated
    • Late stage reaches organs including spleen, kidney, and CNS, disrupts the blood-brain barrier, and releases cytokines such as TNF-α and IL-1β
  • Highest-risk people include those living around Australian flying foxes and those in contact with horses potentially exposed to them.
Pneumovirus

Human Respiratory Syncytial Virus

Core pathogenesis p. 13

  • Replication begins in nasopharyngeal epithelial cells and spreads to the lower respiratory tract.
  • Viremia is rare.
  • Incubation period: 3–5 days.
  • Young children may have high viral titers in respiratory secretions.

Model of RSV pathogenesis in the lungs p. 13

Upper airway ciliated cells→Cell rounding + detachment→Lower respiratory spread→Efficient bronchiolar replication→Cell debris in airway lumen→Airway obstruction
  • Virus and cytokines gain access to airway smooth muscle, promoting inflammation and hyperreactivity and further narrowing the airways.
  • RSV infection of basal cells induces goblet-cell proliferation. Basal cells differentiate, mucus increases, and eosinophils and neutrophils are recruited.
  • Activated neutrophils release neutrophil extracellular traps (NETs).
  • Debris, mucus, inflammatory components, and NETs accumulate in small airways and contribute to obstruction, alveolar collapse, and acute lung inflammation.

Clinical findings p. 13

  • Inapparent infection can begin like a common cold.
  • Pneumonia occurs in infants.
  • Bronchiolitis is especially important in very young babies.
  • Bronchiolitis may progress rapidly and can be fatal.
  • Features include wheezing, dyspnea, tachypnea, fatigue, fever, and cough.
  • Reinfection is common.
  • The lecture connects the name respiratory syncytial virus with the formation of giant cells.

Bronchiolitis, giant cells, and inclusions p. 14

  • Severe infants may require hospitalization because RSV disease can be fatal.
  • The lecture emphasizes many giant cells as typical of paramyxovirus infection.
  • Intracytoplasmic inclusions indicate virus replication.

Mechanism and neutrophil contribution p. 14

  • In severe bronchiolitis, neutrophils undergo degranulation.
  • Released enzymes increase inflammation and promote epithelial cell death.
  • The lecture figure links excessive neutrophil cytokines, degranulation, ROS, and NETosis with lung inflammation, fever, mucus hypersecretion, airway obstruction, epithelial death, and lung damage.

Immunity and reinfection p. 15

  • Maternal neutralizing antibody can protect against lower respiratory tract infection.
  • When maternal antibodies fall after about 2–4 months, severe RSV disease may occur.
  • Primary infection with one paramyxovirus subfamily may induce cross-reactive antibodies to other subgroups.
  • RSV infection does not generate an effective memory response that reliably protects from future exposure.
  • Circulating RSV IgG is present during convalescence.
  • No IgA-producing memory B cells are noted in the lecture.
  • Lack of IgA memory may help explain recurrent infection, especially in childhood.
  • Secretory IgA is found at the epithelial lining of the airways.
Must Know: RSV Memory p. 15
No IgA-producing memory B cells.
The lecture links this lack of IgA memory to recurrent infections.

Laboratory diagnosis p. 15

TestLecture point
rRT-PCRMost commonly used. More sensitive than culture and antigen testing.
Antigen testingSensitive in children but less sensitive in adults.
Viral cultureLess commonly used.
SerologyOften limited to research and surveillance.
Metapneumovirus

Human Metapneumovirus

Pathogenesis and virology p. 15

  • Only metapneumovirus that infects humans.
  • Incubation period: 4–9 days.
  • Viral shedding: around 5 days in children and several weeks in immunocompromised hosts.
  • Replication is limited to respiratory epithelial cells.
  • Cell surface receptor: αvβ1 integrin.
  • Cytopathic effects in cultured cells such as LLCMK2 monkey kidney cells are similar to RSV.

Clinical findings p. 15

  • Symptoms are indistinguishable from RSV and include runny or stuffy nose, cough, shortness of breath, sore throat, wheezing, fever, and rash.
  • Children may have rhinorrhea, cough, fever, and acute otitis media.
  • Lower respiratory illness
    • Bronchiolitis
    • Pneumonia
    • Croup
    • Asthma exacerbation
  • Bronchiolitis is less frequently associated with hMPV than RSV. The lecture cue says that bronchiolitis should still make you consider RSV.
  • Risk groups include children, elderly adults, and immunocompromised individuals.
  • Severe infection can occur in patients with cancer, bone marrow transplants, or institutionalized older adults.
  • Healthy adults often have cold or flu-like symptoms. Asymptomatic infection is more common than for influenza or RSV in this population.

hMPV vs RSV p. 15

FeaturehMPVRSV
Peak ageOlder infant, 6–12 monthsYoung infant, <6 months
SexSlight male predominanceSlight male predominance
SeasonalityFebruary–AprilNovember–January
Clinical symptomsFever, rhinorrhea, cough, wheezing, vomiting, diarrheaFever, rhinorrhea, cough, wheezing, vomiting, diarrhea
Radiographic findingsConsolidation

Laboratory diagnosis and epidemiology p. 16

  • Nasopharyngeal aspirates.
  • RT-PCR assays.
  • Viral antigen detection. Direct immunofluorescence is more sensitive in children and poorer in adults.
  • Ubiquitous and occurs in all age groups.
  • In young children, hMPV infection is less common than hRSV but more common than parainfluenza.
Orthomyxoviridae

Influenza Virus: Genome, Structure, Classification, and Nomenclature

Genome Anchor p. 16
Single-stranded, negative-sense, segmented, enveloped virus.
The lecture repeatedly links a segmented genome with higher mutation potential and reassortment.

Segmented RNA genome and reassortment p. 16

  • A major consequence of segmentation is the ability to undergo reassortment during co-infection.
  • Segments can be exchanged among different viral strains.
  • Reassortment may generate progeny with genes from more than one parent and may confer fitness advantages or disadvantages.
  • Successful reassortment requires compatibility between parental strains, including conserved packaging signals and maintenance of RNA-protein interactions.
  • Influenza has 8 genomic segments. Segment exchange during co-infection can generate new variants.
  • The lecture highlights reassortment between human and avian or swine strains as a mechanism associated with global pandemics.

Influenza structure p. 16

  • Virions are usually spherical but may be pleomorphic.
  • The envelope is a lipid membrane from the host cell.
  • HA and NA are approximately 10 nm glycoprotein spikes.
  • NA is identified as a target of Tamiflu in the lecture.
  • HA and NA determine antigenic variation, host immunity, subtype, and strain designation such as A/H1N1.
  • Protection against reinfection is mainly associated with antibodies to HA. Antibodies to NA are also protective.

Orthomyxovirus types and hosts p. 16

TypeTargetReservoir
Influenza AAvian and mammalian speciesWild aquatic birds
Influenza BHumans and sealsHumans
Influenza CHumans, swine, dogsHumans
Influenza DSwine, cattleHumans

Eight segments and clades p. 17

  • Influenza A is organized into evolutionary lineages called clades.
  • The lecture links clade formation to continuous genetic reassortment and mutation.
  • Clade classification is used to track evolution, assess antigenic variation, and select vaccine strains.
  • The 8 genome segments encode different proteins. The lecture emphasizes that a change in a segment can alter the resulting protein or antigen.

Classification within influenza p. 17

  • Influenza A contains human and animal strains.
  • Influenza B contains human strains.
  • Influenza C contains human and swine strains.
  • Antigenic differences in internal NP and M proteins divide influenza viruses into types A, B, and C.
  • These internal proteins show no cross-reactivity among the three types.

HA and NA patterns by host p. 17

  • Birds: H1–H16 and N1–N9.
  • Humans: H1N1, H3N2, H2N2.

Nomenclature p. 17

  • Type A viruses are subtyped using antigenic variation in HA and NA.
  • Standard isolate naming includes
    • Type
    • Host of origin
    • Geographic origin
    • Strain number
    • Year of isolation
  • For type A, HA and NA are written in parentheses.
  • Host is omitted for human isolates. Example: A/Hong Kong/03/68(H3N2).
  • Host is included for nonhuman isolates. Example: A/swine/Iowa/15/30(H1N1).
  • The lecture lists 18 HA subtypes and 11 NA subtypes recovered from humans and animals.
Influenza antigens

Hemagglutinin, Neuraminidase, Antigenic Drift, and Antigenic Shift

Hemagglutinin (HA) p. 18

  • HA binds virus particles to susceptible cells and is the major antigen targeted by neutralizing protective antibodies.
  • Variability in HA is the primary driver of continuing evolution of new strains and influenza epidemics.
  • HA can agglutinate erythrocytes under certain conditions.
  • Cleavage of HA into HA1 and HA2 by cellular proteases is required for infectivity.
  • The lecture says influenza remains mostly in the respiratory tract because the proteases that cleave HA are expressed there.
  • The amino terminus of HA2 generated after cleavage is required for viral envelope fusion with the cell membrane.

Neuraminidase (NA) p. 18

  • NA acts near the end of the replication cycle.
  • It is a sialidase that removes sialic acid from glycoconjugates.
  • NA facilitates release of budding virions from infected cells.
  • It helps prevent virion self-aggregation by removing sialic acid residues from viral glycoproteins.
  • The lecture suggests NA may help virus move through the mucin layer to reach epithelial target cells.

Antigenic drift vs shift p. 18

FeatureAntigenic driftAntigenic shift
TempoGradualAbrupt
MechanismPoint mutations accumulating at major antigenic sitesGenetic reassortment with an unrelated strain, plus other shift routes taught in the lecture
Main proteins affectedHA and NA surface glycoproteinsHA and NA surface glycoproteins
Lecture framingOccurs as virus passes person to person under different antibody pressuresMay create a mixed strain with pandemic potential
Internal proteinsNucleoprotein does not undergo the antigenic change describedNucleoprotein does not undergo the antigenic change described

Antigenic drift: stepwise concept p. 18

Point mutation→Altered antigenic site→Reduced recognition by existing antibody→Mutant survives and spreads→Further mutations accumulate
  • The lecture uses four antigenic regions on HA to illustrate how antibodies can focus on one region.
  • A mutation replacing one critical amino acid can permit escape from antibodies in one host, after which the mutant passes to another host.
  • Adults with many prior influenza exposures can exert stronger antibody pressure. In immunologically naïve people, including those without prior exposure or vaccination, receptor affinity may decrease.
  • Immunologically naïve means not previously exposed to multiple influenza strains or never vaccinated against influenza in the lecture.

Antigenic shift: mixing vessel concept p. 19

  • Antigenic shift is abrupt.
  • The lecture example sends avian and human influenza strains into a swine mixing vessel.
  • The resulting mixed strain may enter humans and contribute to a pandemic.
  • HA and NA changes can occur independently.

Three shift routes taught in the lecture p. 19

RouteLecture explanation / example
Direct transmission and adaptationAvian virus is transmitted toward humans and adapts. HA receptor binding can change from α2,3-linked sialic acid in avian cells to α2,6-linked sialic acid in human cells. The lecture cites the 1918/1919 Spanish flu as an example.
Genetic reassortmentDifferent influenza A strains co-infect one host cell. Genome segments mix during assembly, creating a third strain containing genes from both parents.
Reintroduction of old strainsA previously circulating strain can re-emerge when population immunity has weakened. The lecture cites H1N1 re-emergence and Russian flu examples.

Direct transmission and adaptation p. 19

  • Highly pathogenic avian influenza A may transmit from birds to humans and then adapt in humans.
  • Mutation can alter HA receptor preference from avian α2,3 to human α2,6 linked sialic acid receptors.
  • A new human strain may then become capable of human transmission and pandemic spread.

Genetic reassortment p. 19

  • A virus adapted to birds or humans can co-infect a pig along with a swine-adapted strain.
  • RNA segments from two influenza A strains can mix during particle reassembly in the same host cell.
  • The resulting strain carries combined genes and may have a different HA and/or NA.
  • The lecture states that pigs and humans possess receptors for both human and avian influenza strains, enabling dual infection.
  • Examples listed include the 1957/1958 Asian flu, 1968/1969 Hong Kong flu, and 2009–2010 H1N1 pandemic.

Re-emergence and additional reassortment examples p. 20

  • When population immunity to a specific strain weakens, an old strain may re-emerge.
  • The lecture cites Russian flu outbreaks in 1950 and 1977 as probably involving re-emergence of the same H1N1 subtype.
Influenza continuation

Life Cycle, Pathogenesis, Clinical Disease, Immunity, Diagnosis, and Prevention

Life cycle p. 20

Receptor-mediated endocytosis→RNP released into cytoplasm→RNP transported to nucleus→Transcription + replication in nucleus→mRNA exported for translation→NP and PB1 return to nucleus→New genome segments produced→HA and NA translated through ER pathway→Genome packaged→Budding
  • PB1 RNA polymerase synthesizes +ssRNA from genomic -ssRNA.
  • +ssRNA templates are copied to make new genome segments.
  • Some new segments serve as templates for more mRNA and later become progeny genomes.
  • HA and NA messages are translated by ER-associated ribosomes and delivered to the cell membrane.

Transmission and respiratory tract damage p. 20

  • Spread is by airborne droplets or contact with contaminated hands or surfaces.
  • Influenza destroys the superficial respiratory mucosa but does not affect the basal epithelial layer.
  • Complete cellular repair may take up to 1 month.
  • Damage to respiratory epithelium lowers resistance to secondary bacterial pathogens.

T-cell pathogenesis p. 21

Infected respiratory epithelial cell / APC→Viral peptides on MHC-I→CD8+ TCR recognition→CD8+ activation→Perforin + granzymes→Infected cell death
  • Activated CD8+ T cells also release proinflammatory cytokines including IFNs, TNF, and IL-2.

Clinical findings: uncomplicated influenza p. 21

  • Symptoms usually begin abruptly.
  • Chills and headache.
  • Dry cough followed closely by high fever for 3–5 days.
  • Generalized muscle aches, malaise, and anorexia.
  • Mild or asymptomatic infections may occur.

Pneumonia complication p. 21

  • A serious complication especially in older adults and debilitated patients with chronic disease.
  • Pneumonia may be viral, secondary bacterial, or mixed.
  • Contributing mechanisms include increased mucus, loss of ciliary clearance, phagocytic-cell dysfunction, and bacterial growth in alveolar exudate.
  • Bacteria listed by the lecture
    • Staphylococcus aureus
    • Streptococcus pneumoniae
    • Haemophilus influenzae

Reye’s syndrome p. 21

  • Acute encephalopathy of children and adolescents, usually ages 2–16 years.
  • Rare disorder that can affect all organs.
  • Most harmful to brain and liver.
  • Includes acute rise in intracranial pressure and massive fat accumulation in the liver and other organs.

Innate and humoral immune response p. 21

ArmLecture components and actions
Innate / cellularMacrophages
Natural killer cells
Dendritic cells
Alveolar macrophages and monocytes activate early and can limit spread through phagocyte-mediated opsonophagocytosis.
HA-specific antibodyMost important for virus neutralization. Binds the trimeric globular HA head and inhibits attachment. Can also help Fc receptor-expressing cells phagocytose virus particles.
Mucosal antibodyIgA and, to a lesser extent, IgM help neutralize mucosal pathogens and reduce entry and replication.

Immunity p. 21

  • Influenza types are antigenically unrelated and give no cross-protection between types.
  • After antigenic drift, pre-existing antibody may still reduce disease to a milder infection.
  • Original Antigenic Sin: later infections or immunizations reinforce the antibody response to the first subtype encountered years earlier.
  • Cell-mediated immunity mainly helps clear an established infection through cytotoxic T-cell lysis.
  • The CTL response is cross-reactive and can lyse cells infected with different subtypes. It targets internal proteins NP and M as well as surface glycoproteins.

Effect of aging on immune response p. 22

Immune cellEffects listed in the lecture
NK cellReduced cell number in weakened health type
MacrophageLower TLR expression
Lower IL-6, TNFα, IL-12, and IFNα production
B cellReduced high-affinity antibody production
Reduced antibody-response diversity
Reduced bone-marrow support for antibody-producing plasma B-cell survival
T cellReduced TCR diversity
Reduced granzyme B production in CD8+ T cells
Reduced IFN-γ production in CD8+ T cells
Lower CD28 expression on CD8+ T cells
Dendritic cellReduced antigen capture
Reduced migration
Reduced T-cell activation capacity

Laboratory diagnosis p. 22

MethodLecture details
RT-PCR and molecular assaysDetect influenza RNA or nucleic acids in respiratory specimens with very high sensitivity and specificity.
IsolationEmbryonated eggs and primary monkey kidney cells are listed as methods of choice.
HemadsorptionCell cultures may be checked 3–5 days after inoculation.
Hemagglutination / immunofluorescenceCulture fluid can be examined after 5–7 days.
SerologyAntibodies develop to HA, NA, NP, and matrix. Routine tests include HI and ELISA. Use paired acute and convalescent sera because many healthy people already have influenza antibodies.

Influenza vaccination options in the lecture p. 22

VaccineAge / route / dose points taught
Inactivated influenza vaccineAdult: 0.5 mL once per season by IM or deep SC.
Children 6–35 months: 0.25 or 0.5 mL once per season per national recommendations.
Age ≥3 years: 0.5 mL once per season.
Repeat after at least 4 weeks in specified previously unvaccinated children.
Inactivated quadrivalent intradermalAdult 18–64 years: 9 mcg once per season.
Live attenuated quadrivalent nasalAdults ≤49 years: 0.2 mL, 0.1 mL per nostril, once per season.
Children 2–17 years: 0.2 mL, 0.1 mL per nostril.
A second dose after at least 4 weeks is listed for previously unvaccinated children in specified age groups.

Final rapid review

Cram Sheet

Fast recall of the lecture’s must-know mechanisms, red-exclamation points, differentiators, timing anchors, and classic associations.

RNA Virus Architecture p. 2
Almost all RNA viruses are single-stranded. Exception in the lecture: Reoviridae is dsRNA.
Segmented RNA virus families recalled in the lecture: Bunyaviridae, Orthomyxoviridae, Arenaviridae, Reoviridae.
Enveloped viruses are more susceptible to chemicals and antimicrobial agents.

Rubella: fastest recall p. 3

  • +ssRNA, nonsegmented, enveloped. One serotype.
  • Postnatal: respiratory replication → cervical lymph nodes → viremia day 7–9 → antibodies and rash day 13–15.
  • Rash: face → trunk/extremities. Usually ≤3 days. No pathognomonic rash feature.
  • IgM: early and gone by ~6 weeks. IgG: persists for life.
  • IgG is the only test for immunity.
  • Congenital triad: heart disease + ocular defects + hearing loss.
  • Earlier pregnancy → greater damage. After 20 weeks, birth defects are uncommon in the lecture.
  • Infant IgM supports congenital infection because IgM does not cross placenta.
  • Live attenuated vaccine. One dose gives >95% long-lasting immunity.

Coronavirus / SARS-CoV-2 p. 5

  • Coronavirus genome: +ssRNA, linear, nonsegmented, infectious, largest RNA virus genome.
  • S: receptor binding and target of neutralizing antibodies. M: central organizer. E: envelope and infectivity. N: nucleocapsid.
  • SARS-CoV-1 and SARS-CoV-2 receptor: ACE-2. MERS: Dipeptyl peptidase 4 (CD26). 229E: aminopeptidase N.
  • Lecture host table: SARS-CoV → bats / civet cats. MERS-CoV → bats / dromedary camel. SARS-CoV-2 → bats / pangolin.
  • Replication occurs in cytoplasm. S binds ACE2 → entry → polyproteins → RTC → replication/transcription.
  • S, E, M assemble with nucleocapsid in ERGIC.
  • Severe disease links to cytokine storm, lymphopenia, viral sepsis, ARDS, increased D-dimer.

Paramyxovirus shared anchors p. 7

  • -ssRNA, nonsegmented, enveloped. Mostly monotypic and antigenically stable.
  • Fusion protein → giant cells / syncytia.
  • F0 must be cleaved for fusion and infection.
  • Replication and mRNA transcription occur in the cytoplasm.
  • Does not undergo antigenic drift.
  • HN neuraminidase activity is present in parainfluenza and mumps and prevents self-aggregation.
  • Syncytium formation is a hallmark.
  • Inclusion bodies are sites of viral synthesis.

Parainfluenza p. 7

CueAnswer
Type 1–2Croup / laryngotracheobronchitis. Barking cough. 6–18 months.
Type 3Lower respiratory spread → pneumonia or bronchiolitis. Young infants <6 months. Most prevalent.
Type 4Usually mild. Most common complication is otitis media.
DiagnosisPreferred NAAT / RT-PCR. Definitive diagnosis by viral isolation in lecture. Serology uses paired sera and four-fold rise.
EpidemiologyDirect contact or large droplets. Highlighted among school children and hospitals.

Mumps p. 8

  • Humans only. Upper respiratory replication → viremia → salivary glands and other organs.
  • Parotitis is not obligatory.
  • Incubation 14–18 days. Saliva shedding from 3 days before to 9 days after gland swelling.
  • One-third may be inapparent but still infectious.
  • After puberty: orchitis may occur. Tunica albuginea tightness contributes to pain.
  • One antigenic type. Permanent immunity after infection.
  • RT-PCR plus paired-serum four-fold rise. IgM = recent infection. IgG = past exposure in lecture.
  • Live attenuated vaccine, commonly MMR.

Measles p. 10

  • Measles = Rubeola. Rubella = German measles.
  • Humans only. Respiratory tract → lymph nodes → primary viremia → reticuloendothelial system → secondary viremia.
  • Rash appears when circulating antibodies become detectable.
  • Koplik spots are pathognomonic.
  • Rash begins on head then moves downward.
  • Most common complication: otitis media.
  • Most common life-threatening complication: secondary bacterial pneumonia.
  • SSPE develops years later and places measles among slow viruses in the lecture.
  • Infection gives lifelong immunity. H-protein neutralizing antibodies are protective.
  • Measles can cause prolonged immune suppression.
  • RT-PCR, ELISA/HI with four-fold rise, or culture showing multinucleated giant cells and inclusions.

Nipah vs Hendra rapid cue p. 12

NipahHendra
Pteropus bats. Pigs important in first outbreak. Raw date palm sap / contaminated fruit are lecture transmission routes.Pteropus flying foxes. Horses are the key bridge to humans.
Symptoms begin 4–14 days. Encephalitis may develop later.Symptoms begin 9–16 days after infected-horse contact. Lung disease and encephalitis possible.
Person-to-person spread after spillover is described.Lecture lists horse-to-horse and human-to-human under species-to-species transmission.

RSV and hMPV p. 15

RSVhMPV
Nasopharynx → lower tract. Incubation 3–5 days. Bronchiolitis in very young babies.Incubation 4–9 days. Only metapneumovirus infecting humans. Receptor αvβ1 integrin.
Debris + mucus + smooth-muscle hyperreactivity + neutrophils / NETs → airway obstruction.Symptoms are indistinguishable from RSV.
Giant cells and intracytoplasmic inclusions.Bronchiolitis occurs but is less frequent than RSV.
Maternal antibody protection falls after 2–4 months. No IgA-producing memory B cells. Reinfection common.Peak age 6–12 months vs RSV <6 months.
rRT-PCR more sensitive than culture and antigen testing.NP aspirate, RT-PCR, viral antigen detection.

Influenza structure and naming p. 18

  • -ssRNA, segmented, enveloped. 8 genome segments.
  • HA binds target cells and is the major protective-antibody target. HA1/HA2 cleavage is required for infectivity.
  • NA is a sialidase that releases budding virus and prevents self-aggregation. It is the Tamiflu target named in the lecture.
  • Type A subtyping uses HA + NA. Example human isolate: A/Hong Kong/03/68(H3N2).
  • Internal NP and M proteins separate types A, B, and C and do not cross-react.

Antigenic drift vs shift p. 19

DriftShift
Gradual changeAbrupt change
Point mutations in antigenic sitesReassortment with unrelated strain or other shift routes in lecture
Accumulates as virus passes through hosts under antibody pressureMixing vessel or direct adaptation may produce novel strain
Common strain evolution / epidemicsPandemic potential emphasized
No segment exchange requiredSegmented genome enables reassortment

Influenza life cycle + disease p. 22

  • Unique lecture anchor: after endocytosis, influenza RNP goes to the nucleus for replication and transcription.
  • PB1 polymerase generates +ssRNA templates from -ssRNA genome.
  • Respiratory epithelial damage lowers resistance to secondary bacteria. Repair may take up to 1 month.
  • Classic influenza: abrupt chills, headache, dry cough, high fever 3–5 days, myalgia, malaise, anorexia.
  • Pneumonia may be viral, bacterial, or mixed. Bacteria listed: S. aureus, S. pneumoniae, H. influenzae.
  • Reye’s syndrome: acute encephalopathy in ages 2–16 with major brain and liver effects.
  • HA-specific antibody is most important for neutralization. Mucosal IgA is important.
  • Original Antigenic Sin: later exposures reinforce response to the first influenza subtype encountered.
  • RT-PCR detects influenza RNA with very high sensitivity and specificity in the lecture. Paired sera are needed for serology.
